title: Basement Window Well Fills With Water or Leaks During Rain: How to Fix the Drainage
question: My basement window well fills up with water every time it rains and it's starting to leak into the basement — how do I get it to drain and stop the leak?
summary: A window well is a below-grade basin, so it only stays dry if water can escape out the bottom AND surface water is steered away from it. Most people just bolt on a cover and stop there, but a cover alone won't fix a clogged or missing bottom drain, soil that slopes toward the house, or a downspout dumping right next to the well. The real fix is a three-part combination: a working gravel drain at the bottom of the well, positive grading and redirected downspouts to keep rain away, and a cover to block direct rainfall and debris. If water still pools after all three, the buried footing drain has likely failed or the water table is high — that's a pro job.

commonCauses.cause: No working drain at the bottom of the well (never installed, or the gravel drain is clogged with silt, leaves, and mud so water can't escape into the foundation's footing drain)
commonCauses.quickCheck: Clear debris, then pour a 5-gallon bucket of water into the well bottom. If it drains away within a couple of minutes, the drain works; if it pools and sits, the drain is clogged or absent.

commonCauses.cause: No cover, so rain, roof runoff, and leaves fall straight into the open well and overwhelm it
commonCauses.quickCheck: Look at the well after a rain — if it's full of wet leaves and standing water and there's no cover, uncovered exposure is a major contributor.

commonCauses.cause: Negative grading or a downspout discharging next to the foundation, funneling surface water toward the well
commonCauses.quickCheck: Set a 4-ft level on the soil next to the well and check the slope. Ground should fall away from the house. Also trace nearby downspouts — if one empties within a few feet of the well, that's the source.

commonCauses.cause: Failed window seal, cracked window, or bad caulk that lets even shallow standing water seep through the frame
commonCauses.quickCheck: With the well drained and dry, run a hose gently against the window frame and watch the inside for seepage; inspect the caulk and weatherstripping for gaps, cracks, or rot.

commonCauses.cause: Failed foundation footing (perimeter) drain or a high water table pushing groundwater up into the well from below
commonCauses.quickCheck: If the well fills or the basement leaks even during dry spells, or after grading, a cover, and a clean bottom drain are all in place, the problem is below grade — a pro diagnosis (exterior excavation or interior drain tile/sump) is needed.

fixes: Bail or pump out the standing water and scoop out all leaves, mud, and silt until you reach the gravel or bare soil at the bottom of the well. A wet/dry shop vac makes this fast.

Find and test the drain: dig down a few inches at the lowest corner to expose the gravel bed and any drain opening. Pour a bucket of water in and watch — quick drainage means the drain works and just needed cleaning; standing water means it's clogged or was never built.
If a drain exists but is clogged, flush it with a hose and run a drain snake/auger down the vertical pipe to clear silt back to the footing drain or daylight outlet.

If there is no drain, create a gravel drain at the low point of the well: dig down at the well's lowest corner to reach the foundation's footing drain, line the hole with landscape fabric, and backfill with clean 3/4-inch drainage gravel so water has a path down and out. Do NOT dig a deep, unsupported hole tight against the foundation — the soil can cave in and you can undermine the footing. If the footing drain is more than a foot or two down, or you can't safely reach it, stop and either tie into a small dry well / drainage basin set below the well bottom or call a drainage pro.

Regrade the soil around the well and foundation so it falls away from the house — aim for about a 6-inch drop over the first 10 feet (the IRC surface-drainage minimum). Tamp the soil so it doesn't settle back into a puddle.
Redirect roof water: add downspout extensions or a buried drain line so every nearby downspout discharges at least 4-6 feet away from the foundation and the well, never beside it.
Reseal the window: scrape out old, cracked caulk and re-caulk the frame with exterior-grade sealant, replace worn weatherstripping, and replace the window if the frame is rotted or cracked.

Measure the well and install a rigid clear polycarbonate cover sized to fit, anchored to the foundation with masonry screws/clips. Clear lets light in; a slight dome or slope sheds rain. Keep it removable from the inside for egress on any bedroom window.
If loose soil keeps washing into the well, add or reset a corrugated metal or composite well liner so the walls hold and debris stays out.

Flood-test the finished job with a garden hose for several minutes, then watch the bottom drain and check the basement interior for any seepage. Confirm again during the next real rain — a dry well and a dry basement wall is what 'done' looks like.
diyVsPro: DIY is reasonable for cleaning out the well, clearing or adding a shallow gravel drain, regrading the soil, extending downspouts, re-caulking the window, and fitting a cover — all above-grade, low-risk work. Stop and call a licensed pro (foundation/waterproofing or drainage contractor) if: water keeps filling the well or leaking into the basement AFTER a cover, positive grading, and a clean bottom drain are all in place (that points to a failed footing drain or high water table needing exterior excavation or an interior drain-tile-and-sump system); you'd have to dig a deep hole against the foundation or tie into the buried perimeter drain; there are foundation cracks with active water entry; or there's more than about 10 square feet of mold. Also call an electrician for any outlet or wiring near the wet well.
typicalCostUSD: DIY: a clear polycarbonate cover runs about $30-150; gravel, landscape fabric, drain pipe, caulk, and downspout extensions add roughly $50-300. Pro window well drain install: about $500-2,500 per well. If the underlying fix is a failed footing drain or a new interior drain-tile-and-sump system, expect roughly $3,000-15,000 depending on scope.
timeEstimate: Cleaning, grading, downspout extensions, and a cover: a half-day to a full day (2-6 hours). Adding or rebuilding a gravel drain: about 1 day per well. Full footing-drain or interior drain-tile work by a contractor: 1-3+ days.
safetyNote: Call 811 (or your local utility-locate service) a few business days before any digging near the foundation — buried gas, electric, and water lines are shallow and hitting one is dangerous. Standing water plus electricity is a shock risk: if any outlet, light, or wiring is near or in the well, shut off that circuit at the breaker and verify it's dead with a tester before working in the water. Do not dig deep, unsupported holes against the foundation — the soil can cave in on you and you can undermine the footing; keep DIY digging shallow and hand off any deep excavation against the foundation to a pro. Window-well liners and covers can be heavy and have sharp edges — wear gloves and lift with help. Water intrusion breeds mold: anything larger than about 10 square feet, or mold in HVAC, should be handled by a professional, and wear an N95 and gloves for smaller cleanups. Keep any bedroom window-well cover openable from inside for emergency egress — never permanently seal it.
toolsParts: Wet/dry shop vac or bucket and hand pump
Round-point shovel and a garden trowel
Perforated PVC or corrugated drain pipe
Small dry well or drainage basin (if you can't reach the footing drain)
Downspout extensions or flexible downspout hose
Clear polycarbonate window well cover, sized to the well
Cover mounting clips/brackets and masonry screws
Non-contact voltage tester (for any nearby outlet/wiring)
Corrugated or composite window well liner (optional)
